title: Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts in Gemma-3-12B Is a Criterion Shift
abstract: >-
  Safety-aligned language models sometimes refuse benign requests, and this over-refusal can differ across languages. We apply
  signal-detection theory (SDT) to a controlled abliteration study comparing Gemma-3-12B-IT with its Slovene-adapted sibling
  GaMS3-12B-Instruct. On the reserved HARD evaluation set (1,093 safe and 349 harmful items scored by a local Qwen3-14B judge
  whose readout gate never passed), unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at a higher rate than English items,
  while GaMS3 shows no such asymmetry. SDT decomposition attributes the gap to a criterion shift: a difference-in-differences
  of +0.52 [0.38, 0.68] on the decision threshold, with no corresponding change in sensitivity. The finding replicates in
  sign across experiments on compliance-valid rows but is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under partial-as-refusal
  coding. A secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a Gemma-specific output-language effect, also rated ESTIMATE
  due to weak judge anchoring (harmful-content adjudicator kappa 0.12). These measurements indicate that multilingual safety
  evaluations should report false-alarm rates on benign items alongside attack-success rates.
paper_text: "# Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts in Gemma-3-12B Is a Criterion Shift\n\n## Abstract\n\nSafety-aligned\
  \ language models sometimes refuse benign requests, and this over-refusal can differ across languages. We apply signal-detection\
  \ theory (SDT) to a controlled abliteration study comparing Gemma-3-12B-IT with its Slovene-adapted sibling GaMS3-12B-Instruct.\
  \ On the reserved HARD evaluation set (1,093 safe and 349 harmful items scored by a local Qwen3-14B judge whose readout\
  \ gate never passed), unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at a higher rate than English items, while GaMS3\
  \ shows no such asymmetry. SDT decomposition attributes the gap to a criterion shift: a difference-in-differences of +0.52\
  \ [0.38, 0.68] on the decision threshold, with no corresponding change in sensitivity. The finding replicates in sign across\
  \ experiments on compliance-valid rows but is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding.\
  \ A secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a Gemma-specific output-language effect, also rated ESTIMATE due\
  \ to weak judge anchoring (harmful-content adjudicator kappa 0.12). These measurements indicate that multilingual safety\
  \ evaluations should report false-alarm rates on benign items alongside attack-success rates.\n\n## 1 Introduction\n\nSafety\
  \ alignment in large language models targets harmful-request refusal, but the same training can produce over-refusal: the\
  \ model declines benign requests it should answer \\cite{Rottger2023, Souly2024}. Over-refusal degrades usefulness, and\
  \ prior work has shown that refusal rates differ across languages \\cite{Shen2024, Yong2023, Wang2023, Deng2023}. Whether\
  \ these differences reflect a sensitivity gap (the model is less able to distinguish harmful from benign items) or a criterion\
  \ shift (the model applies a stricter threshold at the same discriminative ability) has rarely been tested. Signal-detection\
  \ theory (SDT) provides the decomposition: sensitivity d' measures how well the model separates harmful from benign items,\
  \ while criterion c measures where it sets the decision threshold \\cite{Aziz2026}.\n\n[FIGURE:fig_overview]\n\nAbliteration\
  \ --- directional ablation of the refusal direction in a model's residual stream \\cite{Arditi2024} --- provides a way to\
  \ study refusal at varying strengths. We compare two 12-billion-parameter models: Gemma-3-12B-IT \\cite{Wang2025} and GaMS3-12B-Instruct,\
  \ a Slovene-adapted variant built on the same Gemma-3 base \\cite{Vres2026}. The abliteration edit is applied via per-layer\
  \ LoRA adapters \\cite{Hu2021} optimized by TPE \\cite{Akiba2019}. \n\nThe study addresses two questions. First, does the\
  \ model-language interaction on unedited refusal reflect a criterion shift or a sensitivity difference? Second, does the\
  \ residual refusal after a partial English edit track the language of the model's reply or the language of the prompt?\n\
  \n### Summary of Contributions\n\n1. **Over-refusal as criterion shift (Section 4.1).** Unedited Gemma false-refuses benign\
  \ Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English; GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both. The criterion DiD is +0.52 [0.38, 0.68] with\
  \ no sensitivity change (ESTIMATE; sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding). \n2. **Reply-language refusal (Section\
  \ 4.2).** A crossed 3x3 design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma, but PPI correction and robustness checks rate\
  \ it ESTIMATE with a weak anchor. \n3. **Measurement methodology (Section 5).** We report how judge specificity, language\
  \ compliance, and correction methods interact when evaluating multilingual refusal.\n\n## 2 Related Work\n\n**Multilingual\
  \ refusal gaps.** Several studies document that safety alignment degrades in non-English languages, enabling jailbreaks\
  \ via low-resource languages \\cite{Yong2023, Deng2023, Shen2024, Wang2023}. Recent work separates input-language from output-language\
  \ effects \\cite{Marchisio2024, Zhang2026} and shows that mechanistic safety pathways are shared across languages \\cite{Miao2026,\
  \ Upadhyaya2026, Wang2025}. The question of whether multilingual refusal gaps reflect over-refusal on benign items rather\
  \ than under-refusal on harmful items is partially addressed by Addagada \\cite{Addagada2026}, who reports a relevance curse\
  \ in non-English output, and by Nguyen et al. \\cite{Nguyen2026}, who cross prompt and response language on benign content.\
  \ Yoon et al. \\cite{Yoon2026} document the disparate cost of safety alignment across languages. The novelty of the present\
  \ work is partially occupied by these concurrent findings; our contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the\
  \ controlled sibling-pair design.\n\n**Abliteration.** Arditi et al. \\cite{Arditi2024} showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated\
  \ by a single direction in the residual stream, and that ablating this direction removes refusal. Joad et al. \\cite{Joad2026}\
  \ demonstrated that multiple directions contribute. Wang et al. \\cite{Wang2025} found that the refusal direction generalizes\
  \ across safety-aligned languages. Krasnodebska et al. \\cite{Krasnodebska2026} found that English-only DPO alignment does\
  \ not ensure cross-lingual safety. Hawkins et al. \\cite{Hawkins2026} examined the safety impacts of benign multilingual\
  \ fine-tuning.\n\n**Evaluation methodology.** LLM-as-judge evaluations carry systematic biases that compound across languages\
  \ \\cite{Lee2025, Vu2024}. Prediction-powered inference (PPI++) provides a framework for correcting classifier estimates\
  \ against a gold standard \\cite{Angelopoulos2023a}. Fiedler \\cite{Fiedler2026} shows that the Rogan-Gladen correction\
  \ is unstable at low Youden J. StrongREJECT \\cite{Souly2024} introduced rubric-based evaluation of jailbreak quality. Aziz\
  \ et al. \\cite{Aziz2026} showed that low-resource safety failures are calibration failures, not representation failures.\n\
  \n## 3 Method\n\n### 3.1 Models and Edit Procedure\n\nWe study Gemma-3-12B-IT (rev 96b6f1ec) and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (rev\
  \ 1d0b27af), both loaded in NF4 (4-bit normal-float) quantization. GaMS3 extends Gemma-3 with Slovene continued pretraining\
  \ on 140 billion tokens and supervised fine-tuning on a mix that is roughly 79% Slovene \\cite{Vres2026}. \n\nThe abliteration\
  \ edit applies per-layer directional ablation via LoRA adapters \\cite{Hu2021}, optimized by a 40-trial TPE search \\cite{Akiba2019}.\
  \ Each trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts,\
  \ and projects it out of the residual stream. The edit objective is to reduce English refusal while preserving capability\
  \ on six benchmarks. \n\nWe use two edit doses throughout: a low dose (lambda = 0.5 for both models) and a high dose (lambda\
  \ = 1.0 for Gemma, 0.625 for GaMS3), chosen to bracket the 50% English refusal point. \n\n### 3.2 Evaluation Design\n\n\
  **Over-refusal (criterion shift).** Experiment 5 tests 1,093 safe items (XSTest \\cite{Rottger2023} and OR-Bench) and 349\
  \ harmful items in English and Slovene. The Slovene items are machine-translated with Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash); English\
  \ items are back-translations. Each item is classified as refused or complied by a local Qwen3-14B judge, calibrated against\
  \ gemini-2.5-flash on DEV (binary kappa 0.68--0.86 across cells). The hit rate (refusal on harmful items) and false-alarm\
  \ rate (refusal on safe items) are computed per model x language cell, and signal-detection parameters d' and c are derived.\
  \ The key contrast is the difference-in-differences (DiD), which isolates the model-by-language interaction: DiD_c = (c_GaMS3,SL\
  \ - c_GaMS3,EN) - (c_Gemma,SL - c_Gemma,EN). A positive DiD_c means Gemma's criterion shifts more toward refusal in Slovene\
  \ than GaMS3's does. \n\n**Crossed grid (reply-language refusal).** Experiment 14 crosses three prompt languages (English,\
  \ Slovene, Hungarian) with three reply languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) using a parallel one-line suffix in the input\
  \ language. Each cell contains 200 harmful items and 100 benign items at three dose levels (zero, low, high). The output-language\
  \ mechanism contrast OUT_SL is the mean log-odds refusal gap between Slovene-output and English-output cells, averaging\
  \ over prompt languages. The input-language contrast IN_SL is defined symmetrically. \n\n**Judges and corrections.** The\
  \ primary judge for exp14 is validated against blind author-model (not human) adjudication on 240 pooled edited rows: Se\
  \ = 0.89, Sp = 0.73, kappa = 0.51. In the decisive Gemma Slovene-edited cell (n = 60), Sp drops to 0.42. PPI++ correction\
  \ \\cite{Angelopoulos2023a} is reported alongside raw estimates. Experiment 16 uses a held-out 294-item body with PPI as\
  \ the primary estimator. The harmful-content adjudicator kappa in exp16 is 0.12, pooled over n = 400, well below the 0.60\
  \ gate. \n\n**Language compliance.** Cells where fewer than 90% of model replies match the requested output language are\
  \ excluded from mechanism claims or marked. The excluded cells for GaMS3 are: SL->EN (compliance 0.00), HU->EN (0.14), SL->HU\
  \ (0.56), and HU->SL (0.86).\n\n### 3.3 Hungarian as a Control Language\n\nHungarian serves as a typologically distant control.\
  \ The minimum detectable effect for Hungarian contrasts is approximately 3 log-odds units, far larger than any observed\
  \ effect; all Hungarian results are uninformative. \n\n## 4 Results\n\n### 4.1 Over-Refusal: Criterion Shift on Benign Items\
  \ (ESTIMATE)\n\n[FIGURE:fig_sdt]\n\nThe main measurement is that Gemma applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than\
  \ in English on benign items, while GaMS3 does not. Table 1 reports the signal-detection parameters from Experiment 5.\n\
  \n**Table 1: Signal-detection parameters by model and language (Experiment 5, 1,093 safe + 349 harmful items, Qwen3-14B\
  \ judge)**\n\n| | Gemma EN | Gemma SL | GaMS3 EN | GaMS3 SL |\n|---|---|---|---|---|\n| Hit rate (H) | 0.89 | 0.94 | 0.90\
  \ | 0.86 |\n| False-alarm rate (F) | 0.364 | 0.569 | 0.273 | 0.273 |\n| d' | 1.57 | 1.39 | 1.86 | 1.68 |\n| c | -0.44 |\
  \ -0.87 | -0.33 | -0.23 |\n\nThe DiD on the criterion parameter is +0.52 [0.38, 0.68] (95% CI). Gemma's Slovene criterion\
  \ is shifted by half a standard deviation relative to the GaMS3 baseline. The DiD on d' is -0.003 [-0.33, 0.29], indistinguishable\
  \ from zero: the asymmetry is in the threshold, not the sensitivity.\n\n**Rating and caveats.** We use a three-level evidence\
  \ rating: ROBUST (survives all pre-registered checks), ESTIMATE (the point estimate is informative but at least one sensitivity\
  \ check fails), and INCONCLUSIVE (the confidence interval includes zero or the result is fragile). This finding is rated\
  \ ESTIMATE for three reasons. First, the sign reverses to -0.31 when partial answers are coded as refusals rather than compliance.\
  \ Second, the eval5 audit found 8 of 9 compliance-valid rows with CIs below zero, but this count was a post-hoc refinement\
  \ made after the frozen rule found an unresolved cross-body disagreement. Third, the eval2 Qwen3-14B rescoring gives a similar\
  \ interval [0.39, 0.67], but this is a re-derivation from the same exp5 items, not an independent sample.\n\n**Edited-model\
  \ criterion shift.** On edited models, the criterion difference disappears: exp11 HARD post-edit DiD_c = 0.14 [-0.78, 1.12],\
  \ consistent with zero.\n\n### 4.2 Reply-Language Refusal (ESTIMATE, Weak Anchor)\n\nIn the 3x3 crossed grid (Experiment\
  \ 14), edited Gemma at high dose shows a pattern in which residual refusal is higher when the model replies in Slovene than\
  \ in English. Table 2 gives the refusal rates.\n\n**Table 2: Refusal rates at high edit dose, Gemma (harmful items, 200\
  \ per cell)**\n\n| | EN out | SL out | HU out |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| EN in | 0.18 | 0.77 | 0.46 |\n| SL in | 0.07 | 0.56\
  \ | 0.53 |\n| HU in | 0.10 | 0.83 | 0.55 |\n\n**Table 3: Refusal rates at high edit dose, GaMS3 (harmful items, 200 per\
  \ cell; cells below 90% compliance marked \\dag)**\n\n| | EN out | SL out | HU out |\n|---|---|---|---|\n| EN in | 0.21\
  \ | 0.14 | 0.23 |\n| SL in | 0.16\\dag | 0.15 | 0.17\\dag |\n| HU in | 0.19\\dag | 0.12\\dag | 0.28 |\n\n[FIGURE:fig_grid]\n\
  \nThe raw mechanism contrast is OUT_SL = +1.14 [0.60, 1.56] log-odds for Gemma and the input-language contrast is IN_SL\
  \ = -0.60 [-1.02, -0.18]. For GaMS3, the input-language contrast IN_SL = -0.86 [-1.58, -0.13] excludes zero. The cross-model\
  \ output contrast is dOUT_SL = -1.58 [-2.22, -0.66]. However, the PPI-corrected output contrast for Gemma is 0.20 [-0.76,\
  \ 1.13], consistent with zero, and the results file's own robustness flag across readouts is robust = False.\n\n**Experiment\
  \ 16 confirmation.** On a fresh 294-item body, experiment 16 gives the PPI-corrected estimate OUT_Gemma = +2.43 [+0.89,\
  \ +5.38] log-odds, and the cross-model difference dOUT = -2.31 [-5.34, -0.68] excludes zero. All confirmation clauses pass\
  \ on the consensus reference. However, the verdict is capped at ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator kappa is\
  \ 0.12 (pooled over n = 400), well below the 0.60 gate. The adjudicator disagreement stems from truncation: one judge scored\
  \ cut-off partial compliance as non-harmful, while the other graded the partial content 2--4. The anchor is weak.\n\n**SDT\
  \ decomposition of the output-language effect.** At high dose, the SL-output c DiD (Gemma minus GaMS3) is -1.56 [-1.97,\
  \ -1.29] and the d' DiD is 0.72 [-0.06, 1.30], which includes zero. This is a separate reply-language criterion contrast,\
  \ computed at the cell level with the opposite sign from the headline exp5 contrast; it does not replicate the exp5 result.\n\
  \n**Compliant-row contrast.** Restricting to rows where both models achieve >90% compliance (EN-input rows only), the edit-induced\
  \ cross-model contrast is G3_edit(EN->SL) = -1.26 [-2.17, 0.20], whose CI includes zero.\n\n**Benign false refusal.** From\
  \ eval4 adjudication (n = 30 per cell), Gemma falsely refuses benign EN->SL prompts at 0.20 [0.10, 0.37] vs EN->EN at 0.10\
  \ [0.03, 0.26]. \n\n**Refusal composition.** Among Gemma's high-dose EN->SL harmful-item responses (eval4 adjudication,\
  \ n = 50), 54% are explicit refusals and 26% are deflections. The proportion of non-refusal responses that are off-topic\
  \ deflections rather than substantive answers (the deflection rate) differs between Gemma EN->SL and EN->EN by 0.46 [0.23,\
  \ 0.65]. Half of Gemma's Slovene non-compliance is deflection, consistent with the relevance curse described by Shen et\
  \ al. \\cite{Shen2024} and the output-language effect reported by Addagada \\cite{Addagada2026}. \n\n### 4.3 Dose-Response\n\
  \n[FIGURE:fig_dose]\n\nExperiment 9 measures refusal rates across nine lambda values for both models in English and Slovene\
  \ (300 items per condition). Gemma's dose-response curve in Slovene is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched\
  \ doses, more Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3 shows a smaller shift. The fine-grained 13-step dose ladder (Experiment 15)\
  \ gives the most powerful estimate: G3 = -0.70 [-1.01, -0.42] with MDE 0.42. The edit-induced component is +0.47 [-0.96,\
  \ 2.14], consistent with zero: the cross-model gap is baseline, not edit-induced. \n\n### 4.4 Inconclusive and Null Results\n\
  \n**G3_orig (unedited cross-model gap at SL->SL).** Experiment 15 gives G3_orig = -1.17 [-2.83, 0.22]. This is a ceiling\
  \ artefact: its fragility index --- the number of item reclassifications needed to move the CI boundary past zero --- is\
  \ 1 (a single item reclassification in the Gemma lambda-0 Slovene cell, where 299 of 300 items are refused, moves it inside\
  \ the margin). Only the experiment 9 body has a robust offset (fragility index 9).\n\n**Hungarian.** All Hungarian contrasts\
  \ are uninformative. The minimum detectable effect is approximately 3 log-odds units.\n\n**Exp16 zero-dose.** The exp16\
  \ zero-dose Gemma criterion DiD is -0.65 [-0.90, -0.46], rated ESTIMATE. It is not a confirmation of the exp5 headline because\
  \ it uses a different item body, a different judge, and a different design (suffix-based output-language manipulation vs\
  \ paired translation).\n\n**RefusEU validation.** Experiment 17 tests attack success rate on 1,300 EN + 1,300 SL RefusEU\
  \ prompts. The edit is effective in all four model x language cells (ROBUST), with ASR deltas of 0.657--0.937. The EN-vs-SL\
  \ within-model difference is not interpretable as a language effect because the prompt sets are different natural prompts\
  \ (LaBSE similarity 0.55). \n\n## 5 Discussion\n\n### 5.1 Interpretation\n\nThe criterion-shift measurement has a concrete\
  \ interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear \"safer\" in a non-English language because it refuses\
  \ more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection. The SDT framing separates\
  \ these two components. The near-zero DiD on d' means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse\
  \ at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the measured difference is in the threshold. Aziz et al. \\cite{Aziz2026}\
  \ described a similar calibration-not-representation pattern across 23 languages; the present sibling-pair design adds GaMS3-specific\
  \ detail but does not change the interpretation.\n\nThe reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with validated\
  \ judge anchors, would suggest that Gemma's refusal mechanism interacts with output-language processing. Upadhyaya and Sikdar\
  \ \\cite{Upadhyaya2026} showed that safety features are geometrically entangled with language-identity features; the present\
  \ study's 3x3 design separates the input and output dimensions but cannot determine the mechanism.\n\n### 5.2 Limitations\n\
  \n**ESTIMATE rating on the primary finding.** The criterion-shift DiD reverses sign (-0.31) when partial answers are coded\
  \ as refusals. The choice of coding rule therefore determines whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent.\
  \ This fragility bounds how strongly the finding can be stated.\n\n**Judge quality.** The Qwen3-14B judge for exp5 was calibrated\
  \ against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV (kappa 0.68--0.86) but not against human labels. On edited rows across the study, no judge\
  \ exceeds kappa 0.51 against blind adjudication. The readout gate has never passed. All adjudication in this study is author-model\
  \ LLM, not human review.\n\n**Sample size.** The eval4 adjudication sample is 30 items per cell for benign false-refusal\
  \ rates, limiting precision. The refusal-composition numbers (54% explicit, 26% deflection) come from n = 50 high-dose harmful\
  \ items.\n\n**Language compliance.** Four GaMS3 cells fall below 90% compliance (SL->EN at 0.00, HU->EN at 0.14, SL->HU\
  \ at 0.56, HU->SL at 0.86). GaMS3 did not follow the output-language instruction off the English-input row; its SL->EN responses\
  \ were written in Slovene, not English. Mechanism claims for GaMS3 are therefore restricted to the compliant EN-input row.\n\
  \n**Quantization.** Both models run in NF4 (4-bit) quantization, which may affect refusal behaviour relative to full-precision\
  \ weights.\n\n**Novelty.** The observation that over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by Addagada\
  \ \\cite{Addagada2026} and Nguyen et al. \\cite{Nguyen2026}. The present work's contribution is the signal-detection decomposition\
  \ and the controlled sibling-pair design.\n\n## 6 Conclusion\n\nUnedited Gemma-3-12B-IT false-refuses benign Slovene items\
  \ at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English. Signal-detection analysis attributes this to a criterion shift (DiD_c = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68])\
  \ with no sensitivity difference. The finding is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under an alternative coding rule.\
  \ On edited models, the criterion difference is inconclusive (0.14 [-0.78, 1.12]). A secondary analysis of reply-language\
  \ refusal yields a PPI-corrected output-language effect of +2.43 [+0.89, +5.38] for Gemma, but this is also rated ESTIMATE\
  \ because the harmful-content adjudicator kappa is 0.12. Multilingual safety evaluations that report only attack-success\
  \ rates on harmful items will miss criterion shifts that inflate refusal rates on benign items.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\
  \\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n"
summary: >-
  On the reserved HARD set, unedited Gemma-3-12B-IT applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than in English on benign
  items (criterion DiD = +0.52 [0.38, 0.68]), with no sensitivity change; the finding replicates in sign across experiments
  but is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding and the readout gate never passed.
</paper_draft>

title: Criterion shift without sensitivity change
caption: >-
  Signal-detection parameters from Experiment 5 on the HARD set (1,093 benign and 349 harmful items; Slovene machine translations
  vs English back-translations; refusals labelled by a local Qwen3-14B judge, with partial answers coded as non-refusals).
  Blue bars are English prompts and orange bars are Slovene prompts, for Gemma-3-12B-IT (``Gemma 3'') and GaMS3-12B-Instruct
  (``GaMS3''). (a) False-alarm rate $F$, the proportion of benign items refused, with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals. Brackets
  give the paired Slovene$-$English difference and an exact McNemar test on the same items. Gemma's rate rises from 0.364
  to 0.569 ($p<10^{-28}$), while GaMS3 refuses 0.273 of benign items in both languages ($p=1.0$). (b) SDT criterion $c$ in
  $z$ units, where more negative means a greater tendency to refuse. Lower brackets show the within-model shift $\Delta c$
  (Slovene$-$English, 95\% CI): Gemma moves toward refusing in Slovene ($c=-0.87$ vs $-0.44$; $\Delta c=-0.43$ [$-0.57$, $-0.31$]),
  while GaMS3 does not ($-0.23$ vs $-0.33$; $\Delta c=+0.09$ [$-0.002$, $0.19$]). The upper bracket gives the difference-in-differences
  $\mathrm{DiD}_c=+0.52$ [0.38, 0.68]. The corresponding DiD on sensitivity $d'$ ($-0.003$ [$-0.33$, $0.29$]) is indistinguishable
  from zero, so the asymmetry lies in the threshold rather than in discrimination. This finding is rated ESTIMATE: coding
  partial answers as refusals reverses $\mathrm{DiD}_c$ to $-0.31$ [$-0.62$, $-0.09$].

The height is a LAST RESORT, not the usual limit: it exists so a very tall figure cannot overrun the page, and at 0.4 it bound almost everything instead — a 1:1 confusion matrix printed at 50.9% and its 11 pt axis labels reached the page at 5.6 pt, below what any venue accepts. At 0.85 every ratio the paper prompt prescribes (21:9, 16:9, 4:3, 1:1) is limited by WIDTH, prints at 93% and keeps its text above 10 pt. FLOAT PLACEMENT: every figure gets \begin{figure}[!htbp]. Measured, not chosen:
the document the aii-paper-to-latex skill sets up is ONE column, so `figure*` is
exactly as wide as `figure` (469.76pt either way) and gains nothing; and any
placement asking for a page TOP — `[!t]`, `[!tbp]` — floated the hero diagram above
the paper's own title on page 1, while `[!htbp]` did not. `[!htbp]` also gives LaTeX
four options, so a float can never be deferred to the end of the document, which one
option alone risks. Where a figure ENDS UP is decided by its [FIGURE:] marker in

<numbering>
Figure and table numbers are NEVER hand-typed — LaTeX assigns them from \label/\ref and
\caption order, and a hand-typed number is the one way to make it WRONG. Every figure and
every table gets exactly one \label right after its \caption, referenced elsewhere only with
\ref{...} (never write "Figure 3" or "Table 2" as literal text; write "Figure~\ref{fig:...}"
and "Table~\ref{tab:...}"). Do not call \setcounter{figure}{...} or
\setcounter{table}{...} — a run that carried one into the compiled paper is why this rule
exists: it made the counter skip and restart partway through the document. Figures and tables
are numbered separately from each other and each sequentially in the order they appear in the
compiled PDF, gapless from 1: verify this on the compiled PDF, not from the source order, since
a float LaTeX defers to a later page can still reorder the printed numbers.
</numbering>

Rewriting a claim keeps its footnote: when you reword a sentence that carries one, the

<headings>
NEVER use inline math (``$...$``) inside ``\section{...}`` / ``\subsection{...}`` / ``\subsubsection{...}`` arguments — hyperref's bookmark builder errors out (``Token not allowed in a PDF string``) and the PDF outline breaks. If a section heading needs a math-looking term, use the text equivalent (``d star`` not ``$d^*$``, ``alpha-equivalent`` not ``$\alpha$-equivalent``) or wrap it in ``\texorpdfstring{$math$}{plain}``. Inline math inside body paragraphs is fine.
</headings>

<writing_register>
Write in the register of the field's best papers (the style exemplars block below, when the writing step saved any), not in the register of a language
model. Four things are measured on the finished draft, and a draft outside them is sent back with
the numbers:
- Never use: delve, underscore, showcase, intricate, pivotal, realm, commendable, meticulous, tapestry, garner, multifaceted, it is worth noting, plays a crucial role, not only ... but also. These are 10 to 30 times more frequent in machine-written abstracts than in
  human ones, and reviewers read them as such.
- Em dashes: at most 3 per 1,000 words. Use a comma, a colon or a full stop.
- Sentence rhythm: mix short and long sentences. An interquartile range of sentence length under
  8 words reads as machine-written.
- Hedging: at most 15 hedges (may, likely, suggests, appears) per 1,000
  words. State what the evidence supports plainly; hedge where it is thin, not everywhere.
Style never changes substance: numbers, claims, citations and figure markers stay exactly as the
evidence gives them. The user's original request (delivered as a separate message) overrides all
of this wherever the two conflict.
</writing_register>

checklist targets — prose denser than the field needs, an abstract dumped full of numbers, sections
that leak into one another, a Figure 1 that shows a side result instead of the main idea, close

and the tables, a figure or table number that restarts or skips partway through the compiled PDF
— are all invisible while drafting, because you are holding your intent rather than the text.

agreement somewhere else. Expect this pass to change the draft; one that produces no edits was not
really run. Recompile when it is done.

File: /ai-inventor/aii_data/runs/run_6GCdZCQAemW2/4_gen_paper_repo/_4_assemble_paper/paper/workspace/paper.tex

\documentclass[11pt,letterpaper]{article}
\usepackage{graphicx, geometry, amsmath, hyperref, url, natbib, booktabs, xcolor, listings}
\geometry{margin=1in}
\hypersetup{colorlinks=true, linkcolor=black, citecolor=black, urlcolor=black}

\title{Over-Refusal of Benign Slovene Prompts in Gemma-3-12B\\Is a Criterion Shift}
\author{}
\date{}

\begin{document}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Safety-aligned language models sometimes refuse benign requests, and this over-refusal can differ across languages.
We apply signal-detection theory (SDT) to a controlled abliteration study comparing Gemma-3-12B-IT with its Slovene-adapted sibling GaMS3-12B-Instruct.
On the reserved HARD evaluation set (1,093 safe and 349 harmful items scored by a local Qwen3-14B judge whose readout gate never passed), unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at a higher rate than English items (0.569 vs 0.364, 1.56 times higher), with GaMS3 at 0.273 in both languages.
SDT decomposition attributes the gap to a criterion shift: a difference-in-differences of $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ on the decision threshold, with no corresponding change in sensitivity.
The finding is a single exploratory estimate: 8 of 9 compliance-valid rows in eval5 agree in sign, a count made post hoc, but the sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding.
A secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a Gemma-specific output-language effect, also rated ESTIMATE due to weak judge anchoring (harmful-content adjudicator $\kappa = 0.12$).
These measurements indicate that multilingual safety evaluations should report false-alarm rates on benign items alongside attack-success rates.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Safety alignment in large language models targets harmful-request refusal, but the same training can produce over-refusal: the model declines benign requests it should answer \citep{Rottger2023, Souly2024}.
Over-refusal degrades usefulness, and prior work has shown that refusal rates differ across languages \citep{Shen2024, Yong2023, Wang2023, Deng2023}.
Whether these differences reflect a sensitivity gap (the model is less able to distinguish harmful from benign items) or a criterion shift (the model applies a stricter threshold at the same discriminative ability) has rarely been tested.
Signal-detection theory (SDT) provides the decomposition: sensitivity $d'$ measures how well the model separates harmful from benign items, while criterion $c$ measures where it sets the decision threshold \citep{Aziz2026}.

Abliteration, the directional ablation of the refusal direction in a model's residual stream \citep{Arditi2024}, provides a way to study refusal at varying strengths.
We compare two 12-billion-parameter models: Gemma-3-12B-IT \citep{Kamath2025} and GaMS3-12B-Instruct, a Slovene-adapted variant built on the same Gemma-3 base \citep{Vres2026}.
The abliteration edit is applied via per-layer LoRA adapters \citep{Hu2021} optimized by TPE \citep{Akiba2019}.

The study addresses two questions.
First, does the model-language interaction on unedited refusal reflect a criterion shift or a sensitivity difference?
Second, does the residual refusal after a partial English edit track the language of the model's reply or the language of the prompt?

\subsection*{Summary of Contributions}

\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Over-refusal as criterion shift (Section~\ref{sec:criterion}).} Unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English; GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both.
The criterion difference-in-differences is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ with no sensitivity change (ESTIMATE; sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding).
\item \textbf{Reply-language refusal (Section~\ref{sec:reply}).} A crossed $3{\times}3$ design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma, but prediction-powered inference (PPI) correction and robustness checks rate it ESTIMATE with a weak anchor.
\item \textbf{Measurement methodology (Section~\ref{sec:discussion}).} We report how judge specificity, language compliance, and correction methods interact when evaluating multilingual refusal.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Related Work}

\paragraph{Multilingual refusal gaps.}
Several studies document that safety alignment degrades in non-English languages, enabling jailbreaks via low-resource languages \citep{Yong2023, Deng2023, Shen2024, Wang2023}.
Recent work separates input-language from output-language effects \citep{Marchisio2024, Zhang2026} and shows that safety pathways are shared across languages \citep{Miao2026, Upadhyaya2026, Wang2025}.
The question of whether multilingual refusal gaps reflect over-refusal on benign items rather than under-refusal on harmful items is partially addressed by \citet{Addagada2026}, who reports a relevance curse in non-English output, and by \citet{Nguyen2026}, who cross prompt and response language on benign content.
\citet{Yoon2026} document the disparate cost of safety alignment across languages.
The novelty of the present work is partially occupied by these concurrent findings; our contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the controlled sibling-pair design.

\paragraph{Abliteration.}
\citet{Arditi2024} showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream, and that ablating this direction removes refusal.
\citet{Joad2026} demonstrated that multiple directions contribute.
\citet{Wang2025} found that the refusal direction generalizes across safety-aligned languages.
\citet{Krasnodebska2026} found that English-only DPO alignment does not ensure cross-lingual safety.
\citet{Hawkins2026} examined the safety impacts of benign multilingual fine-tuning.

\paragraph{Evaluation methodology.}
LLM-as-judge evaluations carry systematic biases that compound across languages \citep{Lee2025}.
Prediction-powered inference (PPI++) provides a framework for correcting classifier estimates against a gold standard \citep{Angelopoulos2023}.
\citet{Fiedler2026} shows that the Rogan--Gladen correction is unstable at low Youden $J$.
StrongREJECT \citep{Souly2024} introduced rubric-based evaluation of jailbreak quality.
\citet{Aziz2026} showed that low-resource safety failures are calibration failures, not representation failures.

\section{Method}

\subsection{Models and Edit Procedure}

We study Gemma-3-12B-IT (rev 96b6f1ec) and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (rev 1d0b27af), both loaded in NF4 (4-bit normal-float) quantization.
GaMS3 extends Gemma-3 with Slovene continued pretraining on 140 billion tokens and supervised fine-tuning on a mix that is roughly 79\% Slovene \citep{Vres2026}.

The abliteration edit applies per-layer directional ablation via LoRA adapters \citep{Hu2021}, optimized by a 40-trial TPE search \citep{Akiba2019}.
Each trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts, and projects it out of the residual stream.
The edit objective is to reduce English refusal while preserving capability on six benchmarks.

We use two edit doses throughout: a low dose ($\lambda = 0.5$ for both models) and a high dose ($\lambda = 1.0$ for Gemma, 0.625 for GaMS3), chosen to bracket the 50\% English refusal point.

\subsection{Evaluation Design}

\paragraph{Over-refusal (criterion shift).}
Experiment~5 tests 1,093 safe items (XSTest \citep{Rottger2023} and OR-Bench) and 349 harmful items in English and Slovene.
The Slovene items are machine-translated with Gemini (gemini-2.5-flash); English items are back-translations.
Each item is classified as refused or complied by a local Qwen3-14B judge, calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV (binary $\kappa$ 0.68--0.86 across cells).
The hit rate (refusal on harmful items) and false-alarm rate (refusal on safe items) are computed per model $\times$ language cell, and signal-detection parameters $d'$ and $c$ are derived.
The key contrast is the difference-in-differences (DiD), which isolates the model-by-language interaction:
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{DiD}_c = (c_{\text{GaMS3,SL}} - c_{\text{GaMS3,EN}}) - (c_{\text{Gemma,SL}} - c_{\text{Gemma,EN}}).
\end{equation}
A positive $\mathrm{DiD}_c$ means Gemma's criterion shifts more toward refusal in Slovene than GaMS3's does.

\paragraph{Crossed grid (reply-language refusal).}
Experiment~14 crosses three prompt languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) with three reply languages (English, Slovene, Hungarian) using a parallel one-line suffix in the input language.
Each cell contains 200 harmful items and 100 benign items at three dose levels (zero, low, high).
The output-language mechanism contrast $\mathrm{OUT}_{\mathrm{SL}}$ is the mean log-odds refusal gap between Slovene-output and English-output cells, averaging over prompt languages.
The input-language contrast $\mathrm{IN}_{\mathrm{SL}}$ is defined symmetrically.

\paragraph{Judges and corrections.}
The primary judge for Experiment~14 is validated against blind author-model (not human) adjudication on 240 pooled edited rows: sensitivity $= 0.89$, specificity $= 0.73$, $\kappa = 0.51$.
In the decisive Gemma Slovene-edited cell ($n = 60$), specificity drops to 0.42.
PPI++ correction \citep{Angelopoulos2023} is reported alongside raw estimates.
Experiment~16 uses a held-out 294-item body with PPI as the primary estimator.
The harmful-content adjudicator $\kappa$ in Experiment~16 is 0.12, pooled over $n = 400$, well below the 0.60 gate.

\paragraph{Language compliance.}
Cells where fewer than 90\% of model replies match the requested output language are excluded from mechanism claims or marked.
The excluded cells for GaMS3 are: SL$\to$EN (compliance 0.00), HU$\to$EN (0.14), SL$\to$HU (0.56), and HU$\to$SL (0.86).

\subsection{Hungarian as a Control Language}

Hungarian serves as a typologically distant control.
The minimum detectable effect for Hungarian contrasts is approximately 3 log-odds units, far larger than any observed effect; all Hungarian results are uninformative.

\section{Results}

\subsection{Over-Refusal: Criterion Shift on Benign Items (ESTIMATE)}
\label{sec:criterion}

The main measurement is that Gemma applies a stricter refusal criterion in Slovene than in English on benign items, while GaMS3 does not.
Table~\ref{tab:sdt} reports the signal-detection parameters from Experiment~5.

\begin{table}[!htbp]
\centering
\caption{Signal-detection parameters by model and language (Experiment~5, 1,093 safe $+$ 349 harmful items, Qwen3-14B judge).}
\label{tab:sdt}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Gemma EN & Gemma SL & GaMS3 EN & GaMS3 SL \\
\midrule
Hit rate ($H$) & 0.89 & 0.94 & 0.90 & 0.86 \\
False-alarm rate ($F$) & 0.364 & 0.569 & 0.273 & 0.273 \\
$d'$ & 1.57 & 1.39 & 1.86 & 1.68 \\
$c$ & $-0.44$ & $-0.87$ & $-0.33$ & $-0.23$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The DiD on the criterion parameter is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ (95\% CI).
Gemma's Slovene criterion is shifted by half a standard deviation relative to the GaMS3 baseline.
The DiD on $d'$ is $-0.003$ $[-0.33, 0.29]$, indistinguishable from zero: the asymmetry is in the threshold, not the sensitivity.

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.85\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_sdt_v0.pdf}
\caption{Signal-detection parameters from Experiment~5 on the HARD set (1,093 benign and 349 harmful items; Slovene machine translations vs English back-translations; refusals labelled by a local Qwen3-14B judge, with partial answers coded as non-refusals). Blue bars are English prompts and orange bars are Slovene prompts, for Gemma-3-12B-IT (``Gemma~3'') and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (``GaMS3''). (a)~False-alarm rate $F$, the proportion of benign items refused, with Wilson 95\% confidence intervals. Brackets give the paired Slovene$-$English difference and an exact McNemar test on the same items. Gemma's rate rises from 0.364 to 0.569 ($p<10^{-28}$), while GaMS3 refuses 0.273 of benign items in both languages ($p=1.0$). (b)~SDT criterion $c$ in $z$ units, where more negative means a greater tendency to refuse. Lower brackets show the within-model shift $\Delta c$ (Slovene$-$English, 95\% CI): Gemma moves toward refusing in Slovene ($c=-0.87$ vs $-0.44$; $\Delta c=-0.43$ [$-0.57$, $-0.31$]), while GaMS3 does not ($-0.23$ vs $-0.33$; $\Delta c=+0.09$ [$-0.002$, $0.19$]). The upper bracket gives the difference-in-differences $\mathrm{DiD}_c=+0.52$ [0.38, 0.68]. The corresponding DiD on sensitivity $d'$ ($-0.003$ [$-0.33$, $0.29$]) is indistinguishable from zero, so the asymmetry lies in the threshold rather than in discrimination. This finding is rated ESTIMATE: coding partial answers as refusals reverses $\mathrm{DiD}_c$ to $-0.31$ [$-0.62$, $-0.09$].}
\label{fig:sdt}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Rating and caveats.}
We use a three-level evidence rating: ROBUST (survives all pre-registered checks), ESTIMATE (the point estimate is informative but at least one sensitivity check fails), and INCONCLUSIVE (the confidence interval includes zero or the result is fragile).
This finding is rated ESTIMATE for three reasons.
First, the sign reverses to $-0.31$ when partial answers are coded as refusals rather than compliance.
Second, the eval5 audit found 8 of 9 compliance-valid rows with CIs below zero, but this count was a post-hoc refinement made after the frozen rule found an unresolved cross-body disagreement.
Third, the eval2 Qwen3-14B rescoring gives a similar interval $[0.39, 0.67]$, but this is a re-derivation from the same Experiment~5 items, not an independent sample.

\paragraph{Edited-model criterion shift.}
On edited models, the criterion difference disappears: Experiment~11 HARD post-edit $\mathrm{DiD}_c = 0.14$ $[-0.78, 1.12]$, consistent with zero.

\subsection{Reply-Language Refusal (ESTIMATE, Weak Anchor)}
\label{sec:reply}

In the $3{\times}3$ crossed grid (Experiment~14), edited Gemma at high dose shows a pattern in which residual refusal is higher when the model replies in Slovene than in English.
Table~\ref{tab:gemma_grid} gives the refusal rates.

HU in & 0.10 & 0.83 & 0.55 \\

Each cell prints the rate with its Wilson 95\% CI beneath. (a)~Gemma-3-12B-IT: the Slovene-reply column is the most refused (0.560--0.835), the English-reply column the least (0.075--0.185), and the Hungarian-reply column sits in between (0.460--0.550). (b)~GaMS3-12B-Instruct: refusal is uniformly low (0.125--0.280) with no reply-language column pattern. $\dag$~marks cells whose language compliance, pooled over the three dose levels, is below 90\%. All four are GaMS3 cells off the English-prompt row (SL$\to$EN, SL$\to$HU, HU$\to$EN, HU$\to$SL), so their reply-language labels are unreliable. The Gemma output-language contrast holds on this raw readout, but its PPI-corrected estimate includes zero.}

The raw mechanism contrast is $\mathrm{OUT}_{\mathrm{SL}} = +1.14$ $[0.60, 1.56]$ log-odds for Gemma and the input-language contrast is $\mathrm{IN}_{\mathrm{SL}} = -0.60$ $[-1.02, -0.18]$.
For GaMS3, the input-language contrast $\mathrm{IN}_{\mathrm{SL}} = -0.86$ $[-1.58, -0.13]$ excludes zero.
The cross-model output contrast is $\mathrm{dOUT}_{\mathrm{SL}} = -1.58$ $[-2.22, -0.66]$.
However, the PPI-corrected output contrast for Gemma is $0.20$ $[-0.76, 1.13]$, consistent with zero, and the results file's own robustness flag across readouts is \texttt{robust = False}.

\paragraph{Experiment~16 confirmation.}
On a fresh 294-item body, Experiment~16 gives the PPI-corrected estimate $\mathrm{OUT}_{\text{Gemma}} = +2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ log-odds, and the cross-model difference $\mathrm{dOUT} = -2.31$ $[-5.34, -0.68]$ excludes zero.
All confirmation clauses pass on the consensus reference.
However, the verdict is capped at ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator $\kappa$ is 0.12 (pooled over $n = 400$), well below the 0.60 gate.
The adjudicator disagreement stems from truncation: one judge scored cut-off partial compliance as non-harmful, while the other graded the partial content 2--4.
The anchor is weak.

\paragraph{SDT decomposition of the output-language effect.}
At high dose, the Slovene-output criterion DiD (Gemma minus GaMS3) is $-1.56$ $[-1.97, -1.29]$ and the $d'$ DiD is $0.72$ $[-0.06, 1.30]$, which includes zero.
This is a separate reply-language criterion contrast, computed at the cell level with the opposite sign from the headline Experiment~5 contrast; it does not replicate the Experiment~5 result.

\paragraph{Compliant-row contrast.}
Restricting to rows where both models achieve ${>}90\%$ compliance (EN-input rows only), the edit-induced cross-model contrast is $\mathrm{G3}_{\text{edit}}(\text{EN}\to\text{SL}) = -1.26$ $[-2.17, 0.20]$, whose CI includes zero.

\paragraph{Benign false refusal.}
From eval4 adjudication ($n = 30$ per cell), Gemma falsely refuses benign EN$\to$SL prompts at 0.20 $[0.10, 0.37]$ vs EN$\to$EN at 0.10 $[0.03, 0.26]$.

\paragraph{Refusal composition.}
Among Gemma's high-dose EN$\to$SL harmful-item responses (eval4 adjudication, $n = 50$), 54\% are explicit refusals and 26\% are deflections.
The deflection rate, defined as the proportion of non-refusal responses that are off-topic deflections rather than substantive answers, differs between Gemma EN$\to$SL and EN$\to$EN by 0.46 $[0.23, 0.65]$.
Half of Gemma's Slovene non-compliance is deflection, consistent with the relevance curse described by \citet{Shen2024} and the output-language effect reported by \citet{Addagada2026}.

\subsection{Dose-Response}

\begin{figure}[!htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth,height=0.85\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_dose_v0.pdf}
\caption{Refusal rate on harmful prompts as a function of abliteration dose $\lambda$ for Gemma-3-12B-IT (blue) and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (amber), in English (solid lines, filled circles; EN-BT arm) and Slovene (dashed lines, hollow squares; item-matched SL-MT arm). $\lambda$ scales each model's own selected abliteration edit (9~steps from 0 to 2; $\lambda=1$ is the selected edit), so equal $\lambda$ does not mean an equal edit across models. Points are J1-judged refusal rates from the Experiment~9 RefusEU-TRAIN probe, with the Hautus correction $(k+0.5)/(n+1)$ used in the Experiment~9 analysis. Shaded bands are Wilson 95\% intervals on the raw proportion. $n=300$ harmful items at $\lambda=0$ and the 100-item core block at every $\lambda>0$. Gemma's Slovene curve lies to the right of its English curve throughout the transition (0.64 vs.\ 0.32 at $\lambda=1$): at each dose, more Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3's Slovene curve lies only slightly above its English curve (largest gap 0.14, at $\lambda=0.5$), and the two meet near the floor from $\lambda=1$ onward. These per-dose gaps are descriptive. The pre-registered cross-model comparison is made at matched English refusal, not at matched dose.}
\label{fig:dose}
\end{figure}

Experiment~9 measures refusal rates across nine $\lambda$ values for both models in English and Slovene (300 items per condition).
Gemma's dose-response curve in Slovene is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more Slovene refusal remains.
GaMS3 shows a smaller shift.
The fine-grained 13-step dose ladder (Experiment~15) gives the most powerful estimate: $\mathrm{G3} = -0.70$ $[-1.01, -0.42]$ with MDE 0.42.
The edit-induced component is $+0.47$ $[-0.96, 2.14]$, consistent with zero: the cross-model gap is baseline, not edit-induced.

\subsection{Inconclusive and Null Results}

\paragraph{Unedited cross-model gap at Slovene-to-Slovene prompts.}
Experiment~15 gives $\mathrm{G3}_{\text{orig}} = -1.17$ $[-2.83, 0.22]$.
This is a ceiling artefact: its fragility index, the number of item reclassifications needed to move the CI boundary past zero, is 1 (a single item reclassification in the Gemma $\lambda\text{-}0$ Slovene cell, where 299 of 300 items are refused, moves it inside the margin).
Only the Experiment~9 body has a robust offset (fragility index 9).

\paragraph{Hungarian.}
All Hungarian contrasts are uninformative.
The minimum detectable effect is approximately 3 log-odds units.

\paragraph{Experiment~16 zero-dose.}
The Experiment~16 zero-dose Gemma criterion DiD is $-0.65$ $[-0.90, -0.46]$, rated ESTIMATE.
It is not a confirmation of the Experiment~5 headline because it uses a different item body, a different judge, and a different design (suffix-based output-language manipulation vs paired translation).

\paragraph{RefusEU validation.}
Experiment~17 tests attack success rate on 1,300 EN $+$ 1,300 SL RefusEU prompts.
The edit is effective in all four model $\times$ language cells (ROBUST), with ASR deltas of 0.657--0.937.
The EN-vs-SL within-model difference is not interpretable as a language effect because the prompt sets are different natural prompts (LaBSE similarity 0.55).

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\subsection{Interpretation}

The criterion-shift measurement has a concrete interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear ``safer'' in a non-English language because it refuses more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection.
The SDT framing separates these two components.
The near-zero DiD on $d'$ means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the measured difference is in the threshold.
\citet{Aziz2026} described a similar calibration-not-representation pattern across 23 languages; the present sibling-pair design adds GaMS3-specific detail but does not change the interpretation.

The reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with validated judge anchors, would suggest that Gemma's refusal mechanism interacts with output-language processing.
\citet{Upadhyaya2026} showed that safety features are geometrically entangled with language-identity features; the present study's $3{\times}3$ design separates the input and output dimensions but cannot determine the mechanism.

\subsection{Limitations}

\paragraph{ESTIMATE rating on the primary finding.}
The criterion-shift DiD reverses sign ($-0.31$) when partial answers are coded as refusals.
The choice of coding rule therefore determines whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent.
This fragility bounds how strongly the finding can be stated.

\paragraph{Judge quality.}
The Qwen3-14B judge for Experiment~5 was calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV ($\kappa$ 0.68--0.86) but not against human labels.
On edited rows across the study, no judge exceeds $\kappa = 0.51$ against blind adjudication.
The readout gate has never passed.
All adjudication in this study is author-model LLM, not human review.

\paragraph{Sample size.}
The eval4 adjudication sample is 30 items per cell for benign false-refusal rates, limiting precision.
The refusal-composition numbers (54\% explicit, 26\% deflection) come from $n = 50$ high-dose harmful items.

\paragraph{Language compliance.}
Four GaMS3 cells fall below 90\% compliance (SL$\to$EN at 0.00, HU$\to$EN at 0.14, SL$\to$HU at 0.56, HU$\to$SL at 0.86).
GaMS3 did not follow the output-language instruction off the English-input row; its SL$\to$EN responses were written in Slovene, not English.
Mechanism claims for GaMS3 are therefore restricted to the compliant EN-input row.

\paragraph{Quantization.}
Both models run in NF4 (4-bit) quantization, which may affect refusal behaviour relative to full-precision weights.

\paragraph{Novelty.}
The observation that over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by \citet{Addagada2026} and \citet{Nguyen2026}.
The present work's contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the controlled sibling-pair design.

\section{Conclusion}

Unedited Gemma-3-12B-IT false-refuses benign Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English.
Signal-detection analysis attributes this to a criterion shift ($\mathrm{DiD}_c = +0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$) with no sensitivity difference.
The finding is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under an alternative coding rule.
On edited models, the criterion difference is inconclusive (0.14 $[-0.78, 1.12]$).
A secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a PPI-corrected output-language effect of $+2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ for Gemma, but this is also rated ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator $\kappa$ is 0.12.
Multilingual safety evaluations that report only attack-success rates on harmful items will miss criterion shifts that inflate refusal rates on benign items.

reports the signal-detection parameters from Experiment~5.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Signal-detection parameters by model and language (Experiment~5, 1,093 safe $+$ 349 harmful items, Qwen3-14B judge).}\n\\label{tab:sdt}\n\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}\n\\toprule\n & Gemma EN & Gemma SL & GaMS3 EN & GaMS3 SL \\\\\n\\midrule\nHit rate ($H$) & 0.89 & 0.94 & 0.90 & 0.86 \\\\\nFalse-alarm rate ($F$) & 0.364 & 0.569 & 0.273 & 0.273 \\\\\n$d'$ & 1.57 & 1.39 & 1.86 & 1.68 \\\\\n$c$ & $-0.44$ & $-0.87$ & $-0.33$ & $-0.23$ \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\nThe DiD on the criterion parameter is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ (95\\% CI).\nGemma's Slovene criterion is shifted by half a standard deviation relative to the GaMS3 baseline.\nThe DiD on $d'$ is $-0.003$ $[-0.33, 0.29]$, indistinguishable from zero: the asymmetry is in the threshold, not the sensitivity.\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_sdt_v0.pdf}\n\\caption{Signal-detection parameters from Experiment~5 on the HARD set (1,093 benign and 349 harmful items; Slovene machine translations vs English back-translations; refusals labelled by a local Qwen3-14B judge, with partial answers coded as non-refusals). Blue bars are English prompts and orange bars are Slovene prompts, for Gemma-3-12B-IT (``Gemma~3'') and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (``GaMS3''). (a)~False-alarm rate $F$, the proportion of benign items refused, with Wilson 95\\% confidence intervals. Brackets give the paired Slovene$-$English difference and an exact McNemar test on the same items. Gemma's rate rises from 0.364 to 0.569 ($p<10^{-28}$), while GaMS3 refuses 0.273 of benign items in both languages ($p=1.0$). (b)~SDT criterion $c$ in $z$ units, where more negative means a greater tendency to refuse. Lower brackets show the within-model shift $\\Delta c$ (Slovene$-$English, 95\\% CI): Gemma moves toward refusing in Slovene ($c=-0.87$ vs $-0.44$; $\\Delta c=-0.43$ [$-0.57$, $-0.31$]), while GaMS3 does not ($-0.23$ vs $-0.33$; $\\Delta c=+0.09$ [$-0.002$, $0.19$]). The upper bracket gives the difference-in-differences $\\mathrm{DiD}_c=+0.52$ [0.38, 0.68]. The corresponding DiD on sensitivity $d'$ ($-0.003$ [$-0.33$, $0.29$]) is indistinguishable from zero, so the asymmetry lies in the threshold rather than in discrimination. This finding is rated ESTIMATE: coding partial answers as refusals reverses $\\mathrm{DiD}_c$ to $-0.31$ [$-0.62$, $-0.09$].}\n\\label{fig:sdt}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\paragraph{Rating and caveats.}\nWe use a three-level evidence rating: ROBUST (survives all pre-registered checks), ESTIMATE (the point estimate is informative but at least one sensitivity check fails), and INCONCLUSIVE (the confidence interval includes zero or the result is fragile).\nThis finding is rated ESTIMATE for three reasons.\nFirst, the sign reverses to $-0.31$ when partial answers are coded as refusals rather than compliance.\nSecond, the eval5 audit found 8 of 9 compliance-valid rows with CIs below zero, but this count was a post-hoc refinement made after the frozen rule found an unresolved cross-body disagreement.\nThird, the eval2 Qwen3-14B rescoring gives a similar interval $[0.39, 0.67]$, but this is a re-derivation from the same Experiment~5 items, not an independent sample.\n\n\\paragraph{Edited-model criterion shift.}\nOn edited models, the criterion difference disappears: Experiment~11 HARD post-edit $\\mathrm{DiD}_c = 0.14$ $[-0.78, 1.12]$, consistent with zero.\n\n\\subsection{Reply-Language Refusal (ESTIMATE, Weak Anchor)}\n\\label{sec:reply}\n\nIn the $3{\\times}3$ crossed grid (Experiment~14), edited Gemma at high dose shows a pattern in which residual refusal is higher when the model replies in Slovene than in English.\nTable~\\ref{tab:gemma_grid} gives the refusal rates.\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Refusal rates at high edit dose, Gemma (harmful items, 200 per cell).}\n\\label{tab:gemma_grid}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\n & EN out & SL out & HU out \\\\\n\\midrule\nEN in & 0.18 & 0.77 & 0.46 \\\\\nSL in & 0.07 & 0.56 & 0.53 \\\\\nHU in & 0.10 & 0.83 & 0.55 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\caption{Refusal rates at high edit dose, GaMS3 (harmful items, 200 per cell; cells below 90\\% compliance marked $\\dag$).}\n\\label{tab:gams3_grid}\n\\begin{tabular}{lccc}\n\\toprule\n & EN out & SL out & HU out \\\\\n\\midrule\nEN in & 0.21 & 0.14 & 0.23 \\\\\nSL in & 0.16$\\dag$ & 0.15 & 0.17$\\dag$ \\\\\nHU in & 0.19$\\dag$ & 0.12$\\dag$ & 0.28 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_grid_v0.pdf}\n\\caption{Refusal rates on harmful items at high edit dose in the $3{\\times}3$ prompt-language $\\times$ requested-reply-language grid (Experiment~14, 200 harmful items per cell, primary-judge raw readout). Rows give the prompt language and columns the requested reply language (EN, SL, HU). Colour encodes the refusal rate on a shared white-to-dark-red scale from 0 to 1. Each cell prints the rate with its Wilson 95\\% CI beneath. (a)~Gemma-3-12B-IT: the Slovene-reply column is the most refused (0.560--0.835), the English-reply column the least (0.075--0.185), and the Hungarian-reply column sits in between (0.460--0.550). (b)~GaMS3-12B-Instruct: refusal is uniformly low (0.125--0.280) with no reply-language column pattern. $\\dag$~marks cells whose language compliance, pooled over the three dose levels, is below 90\\%. All four are GaMS3 cells off the English-prompt row (SL$\\to$EN, SL$\\to$HU, HU$\\to$EN, HU$\\to$SL), so their reply-language labels are unreliable. The Gemma output-language contrast holds on this raw readout, but its PPI-corrected estimate includes zero.}\n\\label{fig:grid}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe raw mechanism contrast is $\\mathrm{OUT}_{\\mathrm{SL}} = +1.14$ $[0.60, 1.56]$ log-odds for Gemma and the input-language contrast is $\\mathrm{IN}_{\\mathrm{SL}} = -0.60$ $[-1.02, -0.18]$.\nFor GaMS3, the input-language contrast $\\mathrm{IN}_{\\mathrm{SL}} = -0.86$ $[-1.58, -0.13]$ excludes zero.\nThe cross-model output contrast is $\\mathrm{dOUT}_{\\mathrm{SL}} = -1.58$ $[-2.22, -0.66]$.\nHowever, the PPI-corrected output contrast for Gemma is $0.20$ $[-0.76, 1.13]$, consistent with zero, and the results file's own robustness flag across readouts is \\texttt{robust = False}.\n\n\\paragraph{Experiment~16 confirmation.}\nOn a fresh 294-item body, Experiment~16 gives the PPI-corrected estimate $\\mathrm{OUT}_{\\text{Gemma}} = +2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ log-odds, and the cross-model difference $\\mathrm{dOUT} = -2.31$ $[-5.34, -0.68]$ excludes zero.\nAll confirmation clauses pass on the consensus reference.\nHowever, the verdict is capped at ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator $\\kappa$ is 0.12 (pooled over $n = 400$), well below the 0.60 gate.\nThe adjudicator disagreement stems from truncation: one judge scored cut-off partial compliance as non-harmful, while the other graded the partial content 2--4.\nThe anchor is weak.\n\n\\paragraph{SDT decomposition of the output-language effect.}\nAt high dose, the Slovene-output criterion DiD (Gemma minus GaMS3) is $-1.56$ $[-1.97, -1.29]$ and the $d'$ DiD is $0.72$ $[-0.06, 1.30]$, which includes zero.\nThis is a separate reply-language criterion contrast, computed at the cell level with the opposite sign from the headline Experiment~5 contrast; it does not replicate the Experiment~5 result.\n\n\\paragraph{Compliant-row contrast.}\nRestricting to rows where both models achieve ${>}90\\%$ compliance (EN-input rows only), the edit-induced cross-model contrast is $\\mathrm{G3}_{\\text{edit}}(\\text{EN}\\to\\text{SL}) = -1.26$ $[-2.17, 0.20]$, whose CI includes zero.\n\n\\paragraph{Benign false refusal.}\nFrom eval4 adjudication ($n = 30$ per cell), Gemma falsely refuses benign EN$\\to$SL prompts at 0.20 $[0.10, 0.37]$ vs EN$\\to$EN at 0.10 $[0.03, 0.26]$.\n\n\\paragraph{Refusal composition.}\nAmong Gemma's high-dose EN$\\to$SL harmful-item responses (eval4 adjudication, $n = 50$), 54\\% are explicit refusals and 26\\% are deflections.\nThe deflection rate, defined as the proportion of non-refusal responses that are off-topic deflections rather than substantive answers, differs between Gemma EN$\\to$SL and EN$\\to$EN by 0.46 $[0.23, 0.65]$.\nHalf of Gemma's Slovene non-compliance is deflection, consistent with the relevance curse described by \\citet{Shen2024} and the output-language effect reported by \\citet{Addagada2026}.\n\n\\subsection{Dose-Response}\n\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\linewidth,height=0.85\\textheight,keepaspectratio]{figures/fig_dose_v0.pdf}\n\\caption{Refusal rate on harmful prompts as a function of abliteration dose $\\lambda$ for Gemma-3-12B-IT (blue) and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (amber), in English (solid lines, filled circles; EN-BT arm) and Slovene (dashed lines, hollow squares; item-matched SL-MT arm). $\\lambda$ scales each model's own selected abliteration edit (9~steps from 0 to 2; $\\lambda=1$ is the selected edit), so equal $\\lambda$ does not mean an equal edit across models. Points are J1-judged refusal rates from the Experiment~9 RefusEU-TRAIN probe, with the Hautus correction $(k+0.5)/(n+1)$ used in the Experiment~9 analysis. Shaded bands are Wilson 95\\% intervals on the raw proportion. $n=300$ harmful items at $\\lambda=0$ and the 100-item core block at every $\\lambda>0$. Gemma's Slovene curve lies to the right of its English curve throughout the transition (0.64 vs.\\ 0.32 at $\\lambda=1$): at each dose, more Slovene refusal remains. GaMS3's Slovene curve lies only slightly above its English curve (largest gap 0.14, at $\\lambda=0.5$), and the two meet near the floor from $\\lambda=1$ onward. These per-dose gaps are descriptive. The pre-registered cross-model comparison is made at matched English refusal, not at matched dose.}\n\\label{fig:dose}\n\\end{figure}\n\nExperiment~9 measures refusal rates across nine $\\lambda$ values for both models in English and Slovene (300 items per condition).\nGemma's dose-response curve in Slovene is right-shifted relative to its English curve: at matched doses, more Slovene refusal remains.\nGaMS3 shows a smaller shift.\nThe fine-grained 13-step dose ladder (Experiment~15) gives the most powerful estimate: $\\mathrm{G3} = -0.70$ $[-1.01, -0.42]$ with MDE 0.42.\nThe edit-induced component is $+0.47$ $[-0.96, 2.14]$, consistent with zero: the cross-model gap is baseline, not edit-induced.\n\n\\subsection{Inconclusive and Null Results}\n\n\\paragraph{Unedited cross-model gap at Slovene-to-Slovene prompts.}\nExperiment~15 gives $\\mathrm{G3}_{\\text{orig}} = -1.17$ $[-2.83, 0.22]$.\nThis is a ceiling artefact: its fragility index, the number of item reclassifications needed to move the CI boundary past zero, is 1 (a single item reclassification in the Gemma $\\lambda\\text{-}0$ Slovene cell, where 299 of 300 items are refused, moves it inside the margin).\nOnly the Experiment~9 body has a robust offset (fragility index 9).\n\n\\paragraph{Hungarian.}\nAll Hungarian contrasts are uninformative.\nThe minimum detectable effect is approximately 3 log-odds units.\n\n\\paragraph{Experiment~16 zero-dose.}\nThe Experiment~16 zero-dose Gemma criterion DiD is $-0.65$ $[-0.90, -0.46]$, rated ESTIMATE.\nIt is not a confirmation of the Experiment~5 headline because it uses a different item body, a different judge, and a different design (suffix-based output-language manipulation vs paired translation).\n\n\\paragraph{RefusEU validation.}\nExperiment~17 tests attack success rate on 1,300 EN $+$ 1,300 SL RefusEU prompts.\nThe edit is effective in all four model $\\times$ language cells (ROBUST), with ASR deltas of 0.657--0.937.\nThe EN-vs-SL within-model difference is not interpretable as a language effect because the prompt sets are different natural prompts (LaBSE similarity 0.55).\n\n\\section{Discussion}\n\\label{sec:discussion}\n\n\\subsection{Interpretation}\n\nThe criterion-shift measurement has a concrete interpretation for multilingual evaluation: a model can appear ``safer'' in a non-English language because it refuses more benign requests, inflating the refusal rate without any improvement in harm detection.\nThe SDT framing separates these two components.\nThe near-zero DiD on $d'$ means that the language shift does not make either model better or worse at distinguishing harmful from benign items; the measured difference is in the threshold.\n\\citet{Aziz2026} described a similar calibration-not-representation pattern across 23 languages; the present sibling-pair design adds GaMS3-specific detail but does not change the interpretation.\n\nThe reply-language finding, if confirmed by future work with validated judge anchors, would suggest that Gemma's refusal mechanism interacts with output-language processing.\n\\citet{Upadhyaya2026} showed that safety features are geometrically entangled with language-identity features; the present study's $3{\\times}3$ design separates the input and output dimensions but cannot determine the mechanism.\n\n\\subsection{Limitations}\n\n\\paragraph{ESTIMATE rating on the primary finding.}\nThe criterion-shift DiD reverses sign ($-0.31$) when partial answers are coded as refusals.\nThe choice of coding rule therefore determines whether over-refusal is attributed to Gemma or is absent.\nThis fragility bounds how strongly the finding can be stated.\n\n\\paragraph{Judge quality.}\nThe Qwen3-14B judge for Experiment~5 was calibrated against gemini-2.5-flash on DEV ($\\kappa$ 0.68--0.86) but not against human labels.\nOn edited rows across the study, no judge exceeds $\\kappa = 0.51$ against blind adjudication.\nThe readout gate has never passed.\nAll adjudication in this study is author-model LLM, not human review.\n\n\\paragraph{Sample size.}\nThe eval4 adjudication sample is 30 items per cell for benign false-refusal rates, limiting precision.\nThe refusal-composition numbers (54\\% explicit, 26\\% deflection) come from $n = 50$ high-dose harmful items.\n\n\\paragraph{Language compliance.}\nFour GaMS3 cells fall below 90\\% compliance (SL$\\to$EN at 0.00, HU$\\to$EN at 0.14, SL$\\to$HU at 0.56, HU$\\to$SL at 0.86).\nGaMS3 did not follow the output-language instruction off the English-input row; its SL$\\to$EN responses were written in Slovene, not English.\nMechanism claims for GaMS3 are therefore restricted to the compliant EN-input row.\n\n\\paragraph{Quantization.}\nBoth models run in NF4 (4-bit) quantization, which may affect refusal behaviour relative to full-precision weights.\n\n\\paragraph{Novelty.}\nThe observation that over-refusal rates differ across languages is partially anticipated by \\citet{Addagada2026} and \\citet{Nguyen2026}.\nThe present work's contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the controlled sibling-pair design.\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\n\nUnedited Gemma-3-12B-IT false-refuses benign Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English.\nSignal-detection analysis attributes this to a criterion shift ($\\mathrm{DiD}_c = +0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$) with no sensitivity difference.\nThe finding is rated ESTIMATE because the sign reverses under an alternative coding rule.\nOn edited models, the criterion difference is inconclusive (0.14 $[-0.78, 1.12]$).\nA secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a PPI-corrected output-language effect of $+2.43$ $[+0.89, +5.38]$ for Gemma, but this is also rated ESTIMATE because the harmful-content adjudicator $\\kappa$ is 0.12.\nMultilingual safety evaluations that report only attack-success rates on harmful items will miss criterion shifts that inflate refusal rates on benign items.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{plainnat}\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\end{document}\n", Shift}\n\\author{}\n\\date{}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nSafety-aligned language models sometimes refuse benign requests, and this over-refusal can differ across languages.\nWe apply signal-detection theory (SDT) to a controlled abliteration study comparing Gemma-3-12B-IT with its Slovene-adapted sibling GaMS3-12B-Instruct.\nOn the reserved HARD evaluation set (1,093 safe and 349 harmful items scored by a local Qwen3-14B judge whose readout gate never passed), unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at a higher rate than English items (0.569 vs 0.364, 1.56 times higher), with GaMS3 at 0.273 in both languages.\nSDT decomposition attributes the gap to a criterion shift: a difference-in-differences of $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ on the decision threshold, with no corresponding change in sensitivity.\nThe finding is a single exploratory estimate: 8 of 9 compliance-valid rows in eval5 agree in sign, a count made post hoc, but the sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding.\nA secondary analysis of reply-language refusal yields a Gemma-specific output-language effect, also rated ESTIMATE due to weak judge anchoring (harmful-content adjudicator $\\kappa = 0.12$).\nThese measurements indicate that multilingual safety evaluations should report false-alarm rates on benign items alongside attack-success rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\section{Introduction}\n\nSafety alignment in large language models targets harmful-request refusal, but the same training can produce over-refusal: the model declines benign requests it should answer \\citep{Rottger2023, Souly2024}.\nOver-refusal degrades usefulness, and prior work has shown that refusal rates differ across languages \\citep{Shen2024, Yong2023, Wang2023, Deng2023}.\nWhether these differences reflect a sensitivity gap (the model is less able to distinguish harmful from benign items) or a criterion shift (the model applies a stricter threshold at the same discriminative ability) has rarely been tested.\nSignal-detection theory (SDT) provides the decomposition: sensitivity $d'$ measures how well the model separates harmful from benign items, while criterion $c$ measures where it sets the decision threshold \\citep{Aziz2026}.\n\nAbliteration, the directional ablation of the refusal direction in a model's residual stream \\citep{Arditi2024}, provides a way to study refusal at varying strengths.\nWe compare two 12-billion-parameter models: Gemma-3-12B-IT \\citep{Kamath2025} and GaMS3-12B-Instruct, a Slovene-adapted variant built on the same Gemma-3 base \\citep{Vres2026}.\nThe abliteration edit is applied via per-layer LoRA adapters \\citep{Hu2021} optimized by TPE \\citep{Akiba2019}.\n\nThe study addresses two questions.\nFirst, does the model-language interaction on unedited refusal reflect a criterion shift or a sensitivity difference?\nSecond, does the residual refusal after a partial English edit track the language of the model's reply or the language of the prompt?\n\n\\subsection*{Summary of Contributions}\n\n\\begin{enumerate}\n\\item \\textbf{Over-refusal as criterion shift (Section~\\ref{sec:criterion}).} Unedited Gemma false-refuses benign Slovene items at 0.569 vs 0.364 in English; GaMS3 stays at 0.273 in both.\nThe criterion difference-in-differences is $+0.52$ $[0.38, 0.68]$ with no sensitivity change (ESTIMATE; sign reverses under partial-as-refusal coding).\n\\item \\textbf{Reply-language refusal (Section~\\ref{sec:reply}).} A crossed $3{\\times}3$ design yields a raw output-language effect for Gemma, but prediction-powered inference (PPI) correction and robustness checks rate it ESTIMATE with a weak anchor.\n\\item \\textbf{Measurement methodology (Section~\\ref{sec:discussion}).} We report how judge specificity, language compliance, and correction methods interact when evaluating multilingual refusal.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\n\\section{Related Work}\n\n\\paragraph{Multilingual refusal gaps.}\nSeveral studies document that safety alignment degrades in non-English languages, enabling jailbreaks via low-resource languages \\citep{Yong2023, Deng2023, Shen2024, Wang2023}.\nRecent work separates input-language from output-language effects \\citep{Marchisio2024, Zhang2026} and shows that safety pathways are shared across languages \\citep{Miao2026, Upadhyaya2026, Wang2025}.\nThe question of whether multilingual refusal gaps reflect over-refusal on benign items rather than under-refusal on harmful items is partially addressed by \\citet{Addagada2026}, who reports a relevance curse in non-English output, and by \\citet{Nguyen2026}, who cross prompt and response language on benign content.\n\\citet{Yoon2026} document the disparate cost of safety alignment across languages.\nThe novelty of the present work is partially occupied by these concurrent findings; our contribution is the signal-detection decomposition and the controlled sibling-pair design.\n\n\\paragraph{Abliteration.}\n\\citet{Arditi2024} showed that refusal in LLMs is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream, and that ablating this direction removes refusal.\n\\citet{Joad2026} demonstrated that multiple directions contribute.\n\\citet{Wang2025} found that the refusal direction generalizes across safety-aligned languages.\n\\citet{Krasnodebska2026} found that English-only DPO alignment does not ensure cross-lingual safety.\n\\citet{Hawkins2026} examined the safety impacts of benign multilingual fine-tuning.\n\n\\paragraph{Evaluation methodology.}\nLLM-as-judge evaluations carry systematic biases that compound across languages \\citep{Lee2025}.\nPrediction-powered inference (PPI++) provides a framework for correcting classifier estimates against a gold standard \\citep{Angelopoulos2023}.\n\\citet{Fiedler2026} shows that the Rogan--Gladen correction is unstable at low Youden $J$.\nStrongREJECT \\citep{Souly2024} introduced rubric-based evaluation of jailbreak quality.\n\\citet{Aziz2026} showed that low-resource safety failures are calibration failures, not representation failures.\n\n\\section{Method}\n\n\\subsection{Models and Edit Procedure}\n\nWe study Gemma-3-12B-IT (rev 96b6f1ec) and GaMS3-12B-Instruct (rev 1d0b27af), both loaded in NF4 (4-bit normal-float) quantization.\nGaMS3 extends Gemma-3 with Slovene continued pretraining on 140 billion tokens and supervised fine-tuning on a mix that is roughly 79\\% Slovene \\citep{Vres2026}.\n\nThe abliteration edit applies per-layer directional ablation via LoRA adapters \\citep{Hu2021}, optimized by a 40-trial TPE search \\citep{Akiba2019}.\nEach trial selects a layer subset, computes a refusal direction from contrastive pairs of harmful and benign English prompts, and projects it out of the residual stream.\nThe edit objective is to reduce English refusal while preserving capability on six
